en: Revealed his dread majesty,
His eyes reddening like a lion’s.
He was a true marksman,
And his matchlock stood ready.
Just as he raised the matchlock to fire,
The night receded and day broke.
The striped tiger with the ringed tail
Revealed itself as a being of destiny.
Crackling like lightning,
It began to speak in many ways,
Crying out in a mighty voice:
“Fire your gun, Akjoltoy!
Press on without tiring, cunning Joltoy!
I have taken the forms of dragon and tiger
And now stand before you.
To learn how strong and how lionhearted
You truly are,
I tested your mettle.
I transformed into the foremost tiger;
You were a leader of honored heroes,
And before all discerning people,
You were the warrior who faced every foe.
I myself have watched you;
Yes, my son Joltoy, I tested you.
If you wish, I am your blessed Night of Power;
I am the patron spirit who has long supported you,
Who has upheld and guided you.
I am the eye of the seer,
The hero who knows what will come
From six months’ journey away;
I am the eye of the saint.
Do not darken your face as before an enemy;
Lower your gun,
Place your hand upon your breast,
And remain here making your prayer.
What you do would be an outrage;
Open your mouth and repent.
What you do would be reckless;
Stand and think with perfect balance.
Understand well what I have told you;
If you are wise, heed my words.
There is wisdom enough to enter the heart,
She has conceived a craving for tiger.
There is a woman, a fairy-born princess;
Look upon her form and judge:
Say, “This is tiger’s flesh,”
And give Ber­met, dear soul,
This pale walnut as large as a fist.
If she but smells the walnut,
It is far finer than lion’s flesh,
Far finer still than your tiger.
It will satisfy the wings of her craving.
In the desert of Midian,
Where the dragon perished,
Where it scattered its venom,
A single walnut tree sprang up.
If you heed these words,
And, as a sacred trust,
Give this walnut to Bermet,
Her frenzy will subside,
Her eyes will open wide,
Her madness will disappear,
And all her affairs will prosper.
Her people will enjoy surpassing fortune.
When this woman’s craving is fulfilled,
A dark-maned black panther,
Blood-drinking hero Kenen, will be born.
That giant’s name will be Kenen;
He will be the age’s sheltering fold,
The refuge of the Kyrgyz people,
The companion of all living souls.
Slaughter ninety beasts for his feast,
And name him Kenen.
That prince Kenen
Will land upright upon his feet.
Whoever hears his name
Will say, “Calamity has been born,”
And the hearts of envious foes
Will split apart;
Those he confronts will fall,
Those who meet him will be shattered.
“The heir of that mighty champion
Has now arrived,”
Every foe who sees him will cry.
Wherever he charges and lays waste,
All will be smashed and scattered;
Wherever he passes will turn to embers,
He will be a bullet against the foe.
A hero above all heroes,
The black earth will stalk those he hunts.
The gray wolf of the whole wide world,
The renowned hero Kenen he will be.
When Kenen is born,
His radiance will be known to every soul;
Mighty Aigan in Beijing
Will despair of blood and life.
The black Chinese soothsayer,
The great marksman Chongbilgich,
Will recoil in fear and lose hope.
He will let no bustard escape across the plain,
For he is that pale-gray falcon;
He will let no wolf escape in the mountains,
For he is that gray-pouched eagle.
When a day of grief befalls the troubled,
When a night comes that knows no dawn,
He will be the hero who unlocks
The fortune of the fettered marketplace;
He will be the lion who unbinds
The hands of those entangled in sorrow.
He is the hero who will restore their vigor.
God alone grants children;
Put every sorrow away.
In an age of ease and plenty,
Say, “Here my son has come,”
And name him Kenen.
If that child remains alive,
Will he sink when cast into a river?
Will he burn when cast into fire?
Before the insolent, unruly foe,
Would he ever live without wreaking ruin?
His might will reach through many an age,
Disregard this and shame will follow.
This walnut I have brought
I give to Akbermet and Seytek
As a gift held in sacred trust.
This Kertulpar standing here
Was born by supernatural power and has journeyed here;
It is destined for him to mount in war.
For the fierce hero Kenen
This was written upon his brow.
A three-year-old this year, a two-year-old last,
Every mark of a tulpar is complete.
Born by magic and raised in the desert,
Raised upon a dark and rugged ridge,
Raised in a place where neither human, beast,
Nor any living creature ever looked,
It raced the wild asses stride for stride.
With the steeds of bygone mighty Kalmyks—
Kongurbai’s Algara,
Orok Kyr’s Kylkara,
Börüköz’s Kertelki,
And Jaidaksur ridden by the commander—
The warhorses of the giant warriors,
It was born of the same stock
And raced beside the wild asses.
It drank from the Kaimana,
And grazed upon sacred herbs.
The copper hag among horse judges
Who tended it on Mount Barbar
Declared, “This is a true tulpar.”
“This mad creature is like a whirlwind;
Might it take flight?” she said,
And that peerless judge approved it.
Its hoof does not sink into water;
My far-seeing ancestor Körögöch
And my wise father praised it.
When it gathers itself, its stride stretches wide;
By God’s decree and fortune’s aid,
It has been bestowed upon hero Kenen.
Kertulpar will grow into a mighty steed;
Whoever asks to take it will be a stranger.
Broad-lunged and copper-sinewed,
With a wild ass’s haunches and lean feet,
This is the very image of a perfect tulpar.
Roman-nosed and high-crested,
It will not flinch when mounted for battle;
Broad-chested and low-maned,
It will not falter before an open foe.
If, after hardship, its rider cries, “Go!”
No living soul can flee and escape it.
Fail to tell this plainly, and shame will follow;
For Kenen, who is yet to be born,
You must give it, Joltay, as a sacred trust!
The man who had spoken thus
Now vanished from sight.
Leading the entrusted Kertulpar
Unsaddled beside him, he pressed onward,
Praying to the Creator.
That supremely wise sage,
Who had seen distant lands from afar,
Your venerable forefather Joltay
Along a separate, low-lying road
Now turned back—behold him.
Joltay journeyed on and came;
The sheep rustled in their fold,
Light spilled over the earth,
And the world appeared radiant.
Dawn broke as though the earth had split,
Sunlight touched mountain after mountain,
The nightingale sang in the forest,
And the drifting haze dispersed.
Marked waters, stones, and everything else
Stood as plain as five spread fingers.
Just as the world appeared so,
To the palace with its stout gate,
To the fortress with its portals,
Valiant Joltay came.
Without uttering a single word,
He hastened in at a run;
From atop his mountain-like gray horse,
Joltay rushed onward without pause,
With the dignity of a princely pasha,
He entered the palace—
Your uncle Akjoltay.
With uncommon foresight he made his plan;
Turning toward his right,
Without letting anyone know,
Without alerting a single soul,
He leaned aside,
Filled out his robe,
Slipped his hand into his pouch,
And drew out a fist-sized object.
Disregard it and shame will follow:
“My steadfast child Akbermet,
This pale walnut, large as a fist,
The holy wanderer Khizr
Has entrusted to you.
Eat it, my little one;
Your grime-covered heart will open,
And your frenzy will subside.
My child Bermet, heed me:
I have become your healer.
May you be mother of the nation
That bears a lionhearted champion.
Accept your trust, my child,
Purest among women in flowing skirts,
Foremost among women in white kerchiefs.
Eat it, and it will quench your thirst;
Give your great blessing, my child.
Say, ‘My uncle has left me an inheritance’;
Regard this service of mine, my child.”
When Akbermet heard this,
She walked forward glowing,
Shining like the risen moon,
Blooming like a parrot’s plumage,
Revealing the graces of ninety tribes,
That hapless fairy princess.
Her sacred virtue became manifest.
Before dear uncle Joltay
She sprang like a bow and bowed,
With prayer beads hung about her neck,
And pleaded beyond all measure:
“My uncle Joltay, peerless khan,
You who join what has been severed,
Who gathered all these people,
Who mended what was broken,
My undeserved good fortune,
My sheltering presence, my destiny.”
Speaking thus, Akbermet
Bent her neck and trembled,
Imploring her uncle,
Her whole being melting,
Her flesh and nails reaching out.
When he had told her the true tidings,
Her tiny soul cried out,
And she wept in sincere supplication.
